entries.question: Tell me about HealthEcho.
entries.answer:
HealthEcho is a full-stack symptom-analysis chatbot that lets users describe their symptoms in plain text and receive brief health advice generated by a hosted LLM [[cite:1,3]].

**Architecture:** The frontend is built with Next.js 15, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, and it posts to an Express.js backend [[cite:1,3]]. The backend calls Together AI's Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 model to generate the advice, which is then rendered on the frontend with a typewriter animation [[cite:1,3]].

**API Endpoints:**
- `GET /api/health/check` — a simple health check
- `POST /api/analyze/symptoms` — accepts a `{ symptoms }` payload and returns `{ status, advice }` [[cite:1]]

**Engineering details:** The project includes route separation, environment-based secret management, and a polished UI with animated response rendering [[cite:3]].

**Deployment:** It is live at healthecho.vercel.app [[cite:1]].

HealthEcho was built end-to-end as part of self-directed work alongside PersonaQuery and custom LLM evaluation frameworks [[cite:2]].

entries.question: Tell me about JobPilot.
entries.answer:
JobPilot is a multi-agent system that automates the entire job application pipeline, from sourcing listings to tailoring documents and submitting applications. [[cite:1,3]]

**Architecture:** It is built as a five-layer system. Layer 1 contains the individual agents (source, normalizer, match, resume, cover letter, QA, and apply). Layer 2 is a guardrails engine that wraps every agent call with input checks (schema validation, PII detection, token-budget warnings, rate limiting) and output checks (hallucination detection, output schema validation, quality floor, cost tracking). Layer 3 provides skill hooks, Layer 4 handles dynamic orchestration with a priority queue and retry logic, and Layer 5 is a strategic agent that performs weekly performance analysis and recommendations. [[cite:1]]

**Pipeline stages:** The system operates as a 6-stage autonomous pipeline: multi-source scraping (Seek, Indeed, GradConnection via Playwright; Adzuna via REST), LLM normalisation with 0-100 match scoring, tailored LaTeX resume generation, actor-critic cover-letter generation with a 14-point QA gate, and a Playwright form-filling agent that submits applications end-to-end. [[cite:3]] It also includes an ATS detection router that identifies 13 platform types, including Seek-specific session handling and automatic routing of enterprise platforms. [[cite:3]]

**Model routing:** Writing agents (resume tailoring, cover letter generation, strategic role targeting) run on Claude Opus, while routing and utility agents (orchestration, JD scoring) run on Claude Haiku. This selection is deliberate and rate-limit aware. [[cite:1,2]]

**Tech stack:** Python, Anthropic SDK, Playwright for browser automation, Pydantic for schemas, Tenacity for retries, python-docx, and PyYAML. [[cite:2]]

The project is publicly available on GitHub under the repository name JobPilot. [[cite:2]]

entries.question: Tell me about PersonaQuery.
entries.answer:
PersonaQuery is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant that answers questions about Rudra strictly from his own personal documents, including his resume, research paper, patent, transcripts, and project docs, with inline citations and prompt-injection guardrails [[cite:1]]. It powers the "Ask AI" assistant embedded in his portfolio site at rudrajoshi.dev [[cite:1,5]].

**Architecture:** The system has a FastAPI backend deployed on Google Cloud Run and a separate Next.js frontend [[cite:1]]. The portfolio itself is a React single-page site where PersonaQuery is integrated as a drawer, with citation chips that navigate the page to relevant sections and project cards that can pre-fill the assistant with a question about themselves [[cite:5]].

**Retrieval pipeline:** It uses a hybrid approach combining dense embeddings (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 via FastEmbed with ONNX Runtime, 384-dimensional, cosine similarity) with sparse keyword search (BM25 via rank-bm25) [[cite:1,6]]. ColBERT late-interaction reranking (answerai-colbert-small-v1) is also applied [[cite:1]]. The two retrieval signals are fused using Reciprocal Rank Fusion with k=60, chosen because it requires no score calibration between BM25 and cosine similarity [[cite:1]]. Chunking is section-aware with per-document-type profiles: resumes and transcripts use fine 90-110 word windows with atomic bullet grouping, while papers use 220-word windows [[cite:1,3]]. The vector store is a NumPy matrix plus JSONL chunks, with no external vector database [[cite:1,3]].

**Generation:** Answers are produced by Qwen3.8-27B on the Groq free tier (OpenAI-compatible API) at temperature 0.2, with internal query expansion running on GPT-OSS-20B, also on Groq [[cite:3]]. The pipeline is provider-neutral, so switching models is a single-module change; earlier versions used a multi-provider failover chain, then Anthropic Claude, then Hugging Face Llama-3.3-70B [[cite:3]].

**Engineering practices:** The system includes prompt-injection guardrails, per-IP rate limiting, a response cache, retry-with-backoff resilience around the LLM call, structured JSON logging with trace IDs, and latency instrumentation [[cite:3]].

**Evaluation:** An 18-item golden set measures retrieval hit-rate and recall@k, answer keyword match, and citation compliance [[cite:2,3]].

entries.question: What is a Brain-Computer Interface according to the paper?
entries.answer: The documents do not provide a standalone formal definition of a Brain-Computer Interface. However, in the context of the Cognitive-Chair project, BCI is described as a system that uses electrodes to pick up brainwave activity across the standard EEG bands (Gamma, Beta, Alpha, Theta, Delta), where a processing pipeline extracts features and decodes intended movement from that signal, and the decoded command then drives the wheelchair's motor controller [[cite:1]]. The overall architecture follows what is called the general BCI pattern: "sense, decode, act," applied specifically to wheelchair navigation [[cite:1]]. The system is controlled through EEG and EOG signals via this brain-computer interface, replacing the joystick that a conventional electric wheelchair would require [[cite:1]].

entries.question: Explain the Cognitive Chair project and how the EEG/EOG control works.
entries.answer:
The Cognitive-Chair is an AI-based brain-sensing wheelchair designed for paraplegic and quadriplegic users who cannot operate a conventional joystick at all [[cite:1]]. Instead of a joystick, the wheelchair is controlled through EEG and EOG signals via a brain-computer interface (BCI) [[cite:1]].

**How the EEG/EOG control works:**

The system follows the general BCI pattern of sense, decode, and act, applied specifically to wheelchair navigation [[cite:1]]. At a high level:

1. **Sense:** Electrodes pick up brainwave activity across the standard EEG bands (Gamma, Beta, Alpha, Theta, and Delta) [[cite:1]].
2. **Decode:** A processing pipeline extracts features from that signal and decodes the user's intended movement [[cite:1]].
3. **Act:** The decoded command drives the wheelchair's motor controller [[cite:1]].

The project was carried out during Rudra's B.Tech at GSFC University, with co-authors including Kshitij Joshi, Abhilasha Vyas, Smit Joshi, and others [[cite:1,2]]. It received the Best Paper Award at the 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Speech Technology (AIST-2022), organised by the Centre of Excellence – Artificial Intelligence [[cite:1,6]]. The paper was published on IEEE Xplore [[cite:1,4]].

entries.question: How does PersonaQuery's RAG pipeline work under the hood?
entries.answer:
PersonaQuery's RAG pipeline works in several stages:

**Retrieval** uses a hybrid approach combining dense and sparse search. Dense embeddings are produced by `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` via FastEmbed (ONNX Runtime), yielding 384-dimensional vectors scored with cosine similarity, and results are further refined by ColBERT late-interaction reranking using `answerai-colbert-small-v1` [[cite:2]]. On the sparse side, BM25 (Okapi, via `rank-bm25`) handles keyword matching [[cite:2]]. The two result lists are merged with Reciprocal Rank Fusion at k=60, chosen specifically because it avoids the need to calibrate scores between BM25 and cosine, which are not on comparable scales [[cite:2]].

**Chunking** is section-aware and uses per-document-type profiles: resumes and transcripts are chunked finely at 90-110 words with atomic bullet grouping, while papers use 220-word windows [[cite:2]]. The vector store is a NumPy matrix paired with JSONL chunks, with no external vector database [[cite:2]].

**Generation** runs on Qwen3.8-27B on the Groq free tier (OpenAI-compatible API) at temperature 0.2, while internal query expansion uses GPT-OSS-20B, also on Groq [[cite:1]]. Answers must cite their sources with inline `[[cite:N]]` markers, and a cite-only-if-used rule strips any sources the model did not actually rely on [[cite:1]].

**Engineering safeguards** include prompt-injection guardrails, per-IP rate limiting, a response cache, retry-with-backoff around the LLM call, structured JSON logging with trace IDs, latency instrumentation, and a CI pipeline running ruff, the full pytest suite, and an eval gate on every push [[cite:1]]. The evaluation uses an 18-item golden set measuring retrieval hit-rate, recall@k, answer keyword match, and citation compliance, with the CI gate failing the build if retrieval hit-rate@8 drops below 0.90 [[cite:3]].

entries.question: Which project was the hardest, and why?
entries.answer:
Not stated in the documents — no source explicitly ranks projects by difficulty.

**Inference:** Based on the depth and variety of technical challenges described, PersonaQuery appears to be the most complex project. The CV details a hybrid BM25 + cosine-vector retrieval system with section-aware chunking, an identity-query detector to fix a retrieval bug involving wrong-entity contact details, an 18-case golden-set evaluation harness with a CI pipeline that fails the build on regression, an in-process vector store built without an external database, a resilience layer with retry/backoff and circuit breaker, and response/embedding caching [[cite:3,5]]. The combination of retrieval-quality engineering, evaluation infrastructure, and production hardening suggests a broader scope of hard problems than the other projects described in the documents [[cite:3,5]].

By comparison, JobPilot's described challenges center on ATS integration, a cost-tiered LLM strategy, and a React/FastAPI/MongoDB dashboard with CI/CD [[cite:5]], which is technically substantial but involves fewer distinct subsystems than what is documented for PersonaQuery [[cite:3,5]].
